source.title: mSAM: Micro-Batch-Averaged Sharpness-Aware Minimization
source.authors: Kayhan Behdin; Qingquan Song; Aman Gupta; S. Keerthi; A. Acharya; Borja Ocejo; Gregory Dexter; Rajiv Khanna; D. Durfee; R. Mazumder

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Compares training methods and measures test accuracy and sharpness, bearing on generalization and the relationship between sharpness and generalization, with SAM/mSAM methods distinct from the original version-specific tests.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's own reported test metrics for vanilla, SAM and mSAM, the m sweep, Hessian sharpness, and hybrid training. Theoretical claims and cited prior results are not empirical rows. Runtime results are excluded because they measure computation rather than the claim's generalization behavior.
record.test_reason: The study uses the presumed flatness–generalization relationship to motivate mSAM and evaluates its own method. It does not test V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure against train–test gaps or competing generalization measures. Its Hessian eigenvalues measure a different construct. No other version is tested: micro-batch partitioning leaves the effective update batch size fixed, and optimizers are not compared within matched workloads.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors extend a stability framework to argue that mSAM reaches flatter solutions than SAM, report lower Hessian largest eigenvalues for two CIFAR-100 CNNs, and report higher mean held-out performance across their vision and NLP comparisons. They acknowledge dataset and architecture dependence. Their theoretical flatness result does not establish V7's magnitude-aware sharpness–gap relationship.
record.recipe_differences: This paper studies mSAM, compares it with SAM and vanilla methods, and measures Hessian sharpness; it does not reproduce the original magnitude-aware sharpness ranking or train-test-gap analysis in V7.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and architecture affect performance differentiation. In CIFAR100 m sweeps, gains increase up to approximately m = 32, while larger m can worsen results or yield marginal improvements. Small GLUE datasets have higher run variance than larger datasets. Image classification setup varies batch size, model, optimizer and training stage, but is not presented as a controlled generalization-gap comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: mSAM has higher mean held-out scores than SAM and vanilla training in every tabulated vision and GLUE setting; the study notes greater run variability on smaller GLUE datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Micro-batch-averaged sharpness-aware training can improve held-out performance over SAM and vanilla training in these workloads.

fits_no_version.finding: On CIFAR-100, vanilla, SAM and mSAM respectively yield Hessian largest eigenvalues of 26, 21 and 18 for ResNet50 and 92, 30 and 17 for WRN-28-10, alongside increasing test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within these two model comparisons, lower unscaled Hessian largest eigenvalues accompany better test accuracy; this does not establish a magnitude-aware sharpness–generalization-gap relationship.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing micro-batch count improves accuracy up to approximately 32, with deterioration or marginal gains beyond that; hybrid training outcomes depend on architecture.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: mSAM's performance depends on micro-batch count and the portion of training using the method.

record.problems: The paper reports held-out accuracy but generally does not report training accuracy or train-test gaps. The sharpness experiment measures the largest Hessian eigenvalue rather than V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, and does not compare sharpness against measured gaps. The m sweep and hybrid-training results are described qualitatively with figure values not reconstructed here. Results average five independent runs; run variance is explicitly high for COLA and MRPC.
record.rows_left_out: Runtime measurements in Table 5 and Tables B.1–B.2 were left out because runtime is not an outcome bearing on the claim's generalization behavior. Figure B.1's exact point values were not reconstructed; the text-described outcomes are recorded in R48–R49.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the corresponding natural-label and random-label held-out performance.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Matched adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparisons and their dependence on tuning.
Held-out performance as effective update batch size increases under fixed epoch budgets, and recovery of any resulting penalty.
Controlled dropout addition or removal, dataset-size dependence, and underfitting from excessive dropout.
Magnitude-aware weight perturbation tolerance, measured train–test gaps at similarly low training loss, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All tabulated row values match the supplied text. States are cannot_determine relative to the listed claim versions, not because the reported method scores are unreadable. Method-performance rows belong under fits_no_version rather than serving as evidence for version verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD held-out performance under tuning conditions.
Large-batch penalty under fixed epoch budgets and recipe changes.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures; the study measures Hessian largest eigenvalue instead.
